articles.title: Comparative Cardiorenal Efficacy and Safety of SGLT2 Inhibitors and Finerenone in Chronic Kidney Disease With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: No randomized trial has compared SGLT2 inhibitors with finerenone in chronic kidney disease (CKD) with Type 2 diabetes. We estimated their comparative cardiorenal efficacy and safety. MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL and trial registries were searched from inception to August 2026 for placebo-controlled outcome trials. Hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled in a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis, and the between-class contrast was derived indirectly through placebo. Risk of bias followed RoB 2 and certainty followed CINeMA. Ten trial datasets formed a star network without closed loops. Versus placebo, both classes reduced kidney function progression (SGLT2 inhibitors HR: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.56-0.73; finerenone 0.84, 0.77-0.92) and heart-failure hospitalization (0.61, 0.53-0.69; 0.78, 0.66-0.92). Indirectly, SGLT2 inhibitors were favoured for kidney function progression (0.76, 0.64-0.90) and heart-failure hospitalization (0.77, 0.63-0.95), with no significant difference for atherothrombotic events or mortality. The kidney contrast remained significant after excluding high-risk-of-bias datasets, restricting to dedicated CKD trials and applying a uniform endpoint; the heart-failure contrast did not persist in dedicated CKD trials. Finerenone increased hyperkalemia without increasing acute kidney injury. Certainty was low or very low for every between-class comparison. SGLT2 inhibitors and finerenone both provide cardiorenal protection and appear complementary rather than interchangeable. Indirect differences favouring SGLT2 inhibitors derive from a loop-free network with unverifiable transitivity and low certainty; they are hypothesis-generating and should not be used to rank the agents. Safety domains are not reported comparably across classes. CRD420261439899.

articles.title: OSA in Pregnancy: An American College of Chest Physicians Clinical Practice Guideline.
articles.abstract: OSA is associated with significant morbidity in pregnancy. Minimal guidance is available on how best to screen, diagnose, treat, and re-evaluate for OSA in pregnant patients. Considering the potentially adverse consequences of OSA in pregnancy if left untreated, we assembled a panel of experts to review the available literature methodologically and make evidence-based recommendations. Rigorous methodology was applied to provide a trustworthy evidence-based guideline and expert panel report. Panelists developed key clinical questions using the population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) format, addressing specific topics in OSA in pregnant individuals. MEDLINE (via PubMed) and the Cochrane Library were searched systematically for relevant literature and were supplemented by manual searches. References were screened with study evaluation tools to assess for inclusion, to extract meaningful data, and to grade the level of evidence to support each recommendation or suggestion. PICO questions related to screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of OSA in pregnant patients resulted in 9 conditional recommendations made with the evidence available and with the consensus of the expert panel. We recommend screening pregnant patients for OSA, either with a pregnancy-specific screening questionnaire or a standard tool. For those at risk of OSA based on screening, either a home sleep test or in-laboratory polysomnography is recommended for diagnosis. We recommend treatment for those with an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 5 to 15 who have symptoms and sequelae or comorbidities, or those with an AHI of ≥ 15 regardless of symptoms or comorbidities, preferably with autotitrating positive airway pressure. Additionally, scheduled naps may be beneficial as an initial step in alleviating residual symptoms. Reassessment of OSA in the postpartum period is recommended in some patients. Because of the low level of certainty, 9 conditional recommendations were made for the screening, testing, and treatment of OSA in pregnancy.

articles.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy for Glucocorticoid-Induced Dysglycaemia: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Glucocorticoids (GCs) commonly induce glycaemic disturbance, from transient steroid-induced hyperglycaemia to steroid-induced diabetes and contribute to post-transplant diabetes mellitus (PTDM). Insulin remains the standard treatment for GC-induced glycaemic dysregulation. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have a mechanistic rationale here, but their efficacy and safety in GC-induced dysglycaemia have not been systematically appraised. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines (registration number: CRD420251183082). Embase, PubMed/MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched up to May 2026. A structured narrative synthesis was the primary method. Thirteen studies were included, predominantly retrospective cohort studies; 10 enrolled solid organ transplant recipients with PTDM or pre-existing type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 RA therapy, either as monotherapy or as an adjunct to insulin, was associated with reductions in HbA1c and body weight, and a low rate of hypoglycaemia in the majority of included studies. GLP-1 RAs led to insulin dose reduction or discontinuation, reducing injection frequency and treatment burden. Five studies contributed to at least one pooled estimate, and no outcome was informed by more than three studies; given substantial heterogeneity and very low GRADE certainty, these estimates are exploratory and are presented in Supplementary Material 2. Individual studies reported reductions in HbA1c, body weight and insulin dose, with a low rate of hypoglycaemia episodes. However, available data specific to GC-induced dysglycaemia remain insufficient. Prospective controlled trials with explicit characterisation of GC exposure are required.

Effects of a Low-Carbohydrate Diet Combined With Exercise on HbA1c in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Bayesian Multilevel Network and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: The relative benefits of carbohydrate-restricted diets (CRDs) combined with exercise in adults with type 2 diabetes remain uncertain. We compared regimens and explored incremental benefits, dose-response associations and potential effect modifiers. Four databases were searched from inception to 31 August 2026 for English-language randomized controlled trials (RCTs). A Bayesian multilevel model synthesized arm-level changes in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) across eligible post-baseline assessments. An auxiliary frequentist network meta-analysis evaluated network structure and inconsistency; Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) assessed 20 prespecified comparisons. Dose-response and moderator analyses were exploratory. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane tool for randomized trials. Twenty-four RCTs involving 2038 participants were included. Compared with pooled active/passive controls, aerobic training plus a moderately low-carbohydrate diet was associated with lower HbA1c (posterior median mean difference, -0.53 percentage points; 95% credible interval, -0.76 to -0.28). Estimates for other combined regimens were less precise. The auxiliary network had two disconnected components, and confidence was very low for all 20 assessed comparisons. Under the specified priors, the Bayes factor favoured the model without treatment-specific effects (BF10 = 0.034). Higher prescribed exercise doses were associated with larger reductions versus pooled controls, but an incremental benefit over exercise or CRD alone was not established. Matched carbohydrate-dose contrasts were imprecise. Limitations of the arm-level model, sparse evidence and very low confidence in the assessed auxiliary-network comparisons leave comparative benefits uncertain. The findings do not establish a preferred regimen, an incremental benefit over either component alone, or a specific dietary or exercise prescription.

Safety of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors in Older Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) have demonstrated cardiorenal benefits in individuals with type 2 diabetes, but safety data in older adults remain limited. We evaluated the real-world safety of SGLT2is compared with dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors (DPP-4is) among individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes. We conducted a population-based, active-comparator, new-user cohort study using administrative health databases from British Columbia, Canada. We included individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes initiating SGLT2is or DPP-4is between 1 January 2021 and 31 December 2023. Primary outcomes were infection, diabetic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury, fall, fracture, and all-cause hospitalization. Cox regression with propensity score-based standardized mortality ratio weighting was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). The study included 4,997 SGLT2i initiators (median age, 79 years; 37% women) and 1,289 DPP-4i initiators (median age, 82 years; 50% women). Compared with DPP-4i initiation, SGLT2i initiation was associated with lower risks of acute kidney injury (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60-0.95) and all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77-0.98), with no difference in risk of infection. No differences were observed in risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, falls, or fractures, although CIs were compatible with both benefit and harm. In individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2i initiation was not associated with increased risk of harm compared with DPP-4i initiation, although estimates were imprecise for some outcomes. These findings may support consideration of SGLT2is as a treatment option in this population.

articles.title: Antithrombotic Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: The SIMPLAAFY Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Following a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) procedure, antithrombotic therapy is administered to safely allow time for device endothelialization. However, the optimal postimplant antithrombotic regimen is unknown. To determine if either reduced-dose non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) or aspirin alone are noninferior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for the composite clinical end point of death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding through 6 months post LAAC. This open-label, 3-group, multicenter clinical trial randomized 1857 patients between October 2024 and December 2025 at 87 US investigational sites, with the final 6-month follow-up in July 2026. Enrolled patients had nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, underwent successful LAAC, and were eligible for all 3 regimens. Patients were randomly allocated 1:1:1 to DAPT for 6 months followed by aspirin (n = 624), a reduced-dose NOAC for 3 months followed by aspirin (n = 620), or aspirin alone for 12 months (n = 613). The primary outcome was the 6-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding. Noninferiority was tested in the primary analysis population with a 1-sided Farrington-Manning test (α = .025). Bleeding and 45-day device-related thrombus rates were exploratory without multiplicity adjustment. The cohort had a mean age of 76 (SD, 8) years, 42.9% were female, the mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.2 (SD, 1.3), and 68.0% had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome occurred in 41 patients (6.9%) with DAPT vs 31 (5.1%) with a reduced-dose NOAC (risk ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.48-1.18]; risk difference, -1.7 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, 1.2) and 20 (3.3%) with aspirin alone (risk ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.29-0.82]; risk difference, -3.5 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, -0.8). Both monotherapy strategies met noninferiority criteria (P < .001 for noninferiority for both). Major bleeding was 4.5% with DAPT, 2.7% with reduced-dose NOACs, and 1.7% with aspirin alone; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 8.7%, 4.8%, and 3.8%, respectively. Device-related thrombus was observed in 3.4%, 0.9%, and 2.7%, respectively. Both reduced-dose NOACs and aspirin alone were noninferior to DAPT for 6-month outcomes after uncomplicated LAAC. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06521463.

articles.title: Single Intranasal Administration of the Psychedelic Mebufotenin for Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Psychedelics represent a potential breakthrough for treatment-resistant depression; however, the prolonged in-clinic monitoring required for compounds such as psilocybin and lysergic acid diethylamide is a logistical hurdle to widespread use. Intranasal mebufotenin (5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine), a 5-hydroxytryptamine 1A (5-HT1A) and 5-HT2A agonist associated with brief psychedelic experiences, may address this limitation. To evaluate the safety, efficacy, and time to discharge readiness following a single dose of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate in adults with treatment-resistant depression. Phase 2b, randomized, double-blind trial with an 8-week blinded follow-up conducted between September 2023 and April 2025 at 38 sites in Australia, Europe, and the US. Participants were aged 18 to 75 years with moderate to severe major depressive disorder nonresponsive to 2 to 5 antidepressant trials in the current episode. The last date of follow-up was April 28, 2025. After antidepressant washout as needed, participants were randomly assigned to receive a single dose of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate, 8 mg (n = 46), 12 mg (n = 73), or 0.3 mg (a low-dose comparator; n = 74), alongside psychological support. The primary end point was total score change on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS; score range, 0-60; higher scores indicate more severe depression) from baseline to day 29 in the 12-mg vs 0.3-mg dose groups. Eighteen secondary end points were assessed for the 12-mg and 8-mg vs 0.3-mg doses. Discharge readiness was assessed starting 90 minutes after dosing. Among the 193 included participants, the mean age was 41 (SD, 11.1) years and 59.1% were female. From baseline to day 29, treatment with 12-mg intranasal mebufotenin benzoate vs the 0.3-mg dose (the primary end point) was associated with significantly reduced MADRS scores (mean score change, -11.1 [SD, 11.6] vs -5.5 [SD, 9.9], respectively; mean difference, -5.3 [95% CI, -8.9 to -1.8]; P = .003). The 8-mg dose also led to reduced scores from baseline to day 29 (mean score change, -12.5 [SD, 12.7]) vs the 0.3-mg dose (mean difference, -6.2 [95% CI, -10.2 to -2.1]; P = .003). MADRS reductions with the 8-mg and 12-mg doses were similar and significantly greater at all other time points from 2 to 57 days post dose vs the 0.3-mg dose. Day 29 response rates were 35%, 34%, and 12% and remission rates were 26%, 18%, and 8% in the 8-mg, 12-mg, and 0.3-mg dose groups, respectively. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 76%, 85%, and 73% of participants in the 8-mg, 12-mg, and 0.3-mg dose groups, respectively; most events (99.7%) were mild or moderate. Overall, most participants were deemed ready for discharge within 2 hours post dose (85% for 8 mg and 78% for 12 mg). In adults with treatment-resistant depression, single doses of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate were well tolerated and produced rapid, robust, and durable reductions in depressive symptoms. Intranasal mebufotenin benzoate may improve treatment access and convenience, requiring a shorter monitoring period and fewer clinic visits compared with psilocybin and esketamine, respectively. articles.title: Thrombolysis in the Delayed Treatment Window for Acute Ischemic Stroke: Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Intravenous thrombolysis is a standard treatment for acute ischemic stroke but has traditionally been limited to 4.5 hours after symptom onset. This time-based restriction may exclude patients with salvageable brain tissue, especially those with wake-up or unknown-onset strokes. articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of CagriSema in Type 2 Diabetes: A Dose- and Comparator-Specific Systematic Review and Bayesian Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: CagriSema combines cagrilintide with semaglutide and may improve glycaemic control and body weight in Type 2 diabetes. We evaluated its dose- and comparator-specific efficacy and safety. PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched through 30 June 2026 for randomized controlled trials. Analyses were stratified by CagriSema dose and comparator. For HbA1c and body weight, efficacy/trial-product estimands were aligned where sufficiently reported, with treatment-policy estimates examined in sensitivity analyses. Bayesian random-effects models generated posterior medians and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). Six trials representing 4554 potentially eligible participants with Type 2 diabetes were included. Compared with placebo, CagriSema 2.4 mg produced between-group differences of -1.87 percentage points in HbA1c (95% CrI, -2.08 to -1.62) and -12.69 percentage points in percentage body-weight change (95% CrI, -13.78 to -11.61). Versus semaglutide 2.4 mg, the additional HbA1c reduction was modest and uncertain (-0.21 percentage points; 95% CrI, -0.62 to 0.11), whereas additional body-weight reduction remained probable (-5.84 percentage points; 95% CrI, -10.08 to -2.15). Gastrointestinal adverse events and adverse-event-related discontinuation were increased versus placebo (RR, 2.27 [95% CrI, 1.81 - 3.00] and 3.16 [1.50 to 6.87], respectively), while estimates versus semaglutide were less precise. CagriSema provides substantial glycaemic and body-weight benefits versus placebo. Its incremental advantage over dose-matched semaglutide is more evident for body-weight reduction, while comparative gastrointestinal tolerability and discontinuation risk remain uncertain.

articles.title: Bleeding With Asundexian Versus Placebo in Patients With Noncardioembolic Ischemic Stroke or High-Risk TIA: OCEANIC-STROKE Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: OCEANIC-STROKE (XXX) showed that asundexian added to antiplatelet therapy reduced ischemic stroke without significantly increasing bleeding in patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack. While-on-treatment analyses included events through 2 days after the last dose, with death and permanent discontinuation as competing risks. Major bleeding occurred in 117 (1.9%) participants with asundexian and 107 (1.7%) with placebo (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR], 1.10 [95% CI, 0.85-1.44]; =0.46). Major or CRNM bleeding occurred in 339 (5.5%) and 307 (5.0%), respectively (csHR, 1.12 [95% CI, 0.96-1.30]; =0.16), and any bleeding in 763 (12.5%) and 752 (12.3%) (csHR, 1.02 [95% CI, 0.93-1.13]; =0.65). Treatment effects for major and major or CRNM bleeding were consistent across prespecified subgroups, including planned dual antiplatelet therapy. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 41 (0.7%) and 36 (0.6%) participants. Any gastrointestinal bleeding occurred in 186 (3.0%) and 147 (2.4%) (csHR, 1.28 [95% CI, 1.03-1.59]), and lower gastrointestinal bleeding in 102 (1.7%) and 59 (1.0%) (csHR, 1.75 [95% CI, 1.27-2.41]), primarily rectal bleeding. Any procedure-related bleeding and any mucosal bleeding did not differ significantly. Asundexian added to antiplatelet therapy reduced ischemic stroke without significantly increasing major, major or CRNM, or any bleeding. Lower gastrointestinal bleeding was more frequent with asundexian, whereas treatment effects on major and major or CRNM bleeding were consistent across prespecified subgroups. articles.title: Curcumin Suppresses Growth of Recurrent Colorectal Adenoma After Endoscopic Resection: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Multicenter Trial.
articles.abstract: Experimental and limited clinical studies suggest that curcumin has chemopreventive activity in the colorectum. This large-scale clinical trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of curcumin in patients with previously endoscopically resected colorectal neoplasia. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trial enrolled patients with previously resected colorectal neoplasia. Eligible patients were randomly assigned (1:1), using a stratified, computer-generated scheme to receive oral submicron-powdered curcumin (Theracurmin; 180 mg twice daily) or identical placebo capsules for 2 years. All analyses were performed according to a modified intention-to-treat principle including all randomly assigned patients who underwent the 2-year colonoscopy. Between April 1, 2016, and March 31, 2020, 577 patients were randomly assigned to curcumin (n = 287) or placebo groups (n = 290). The detection rate of recurrent colorectal adenomas at 2 years, the primary end point, did not differ significantly between groups (risk ratio 0.98; 95% confident interval 0.82-1.16). However, the detection rate of adenomas ≥6 mm, a prespecified lesion category recommended for endoscopic resection in Japanese guidelines, was significantly lower with curcumin (risk ratio, 0.56; 95% confident interval, 0.33-0.95; P = 0.04). The per-patient number of adenomas ≥6 mm was also significantly lower ( P = 0.03), and the median size of all detected adenomas was significantly smaller in the curcumin group ( P = 0.003). The inhibitory effect seemed more pronounced in patients with higher baseline adenoma burden and in men in exploratory analyses. Treatment-related adverse events were infrequent and mild. Curcumin inhibited the growth of recurrent colorectal adenomas, despite no significant reduction in the overall incidence of recurrence. This is the first large-scale randomized clinical trial demonstrating the suppressive efficacy of curcumin against colorectal neoplasia, and also highlighting the importance of incorporating growth-related endpoints, in addition to incidence-based or detection-based end points, in chemoprevention studies (jRCTs061180079).

articles.title: Remibrutinib versus teriflunomide in relapsing multiple sclerosis (REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2): two randomised, phase 3 trials.
articles.abstract: Remibrutinib is a highly selective, potent, covalent, CNS-penetrant, oral BTK inhibitor. We assessed the efficacy and safety of remibrutinib in adult patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2 are two identical, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active comparator-controlled, parallel-group, event-driven, phase 3 trials conducted at 407 centres in 46 countries. Patients aged 18-55 years with relapsing multiple sclerosis, an Expanded Disability Status Scale score of 0-5·5, and evidence of recent disease activity were randomly assigned 1:1 to oral remibrutinib 100 mg twice daily or teriflunomide 14 mg once daily via interactive response technology. Randomisation was stratified by geographical region, MRI cohort participation, and multiple sclerosis subtype. Patients, site investigators, and trial team were masked to treatment allocation. The primary endpoint was annualised relapse rate (ARR), defined as the number of confirmed multiple sclerosis relapses per patient-year with up to 30 months of follow-up, and assessed in all randomly assigned patients. These trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05147220 and NCT05156281) and are ongoing, not recruiting. Between Dec 13, 2021, and Dec 30, 2025, 2632 patients were screened and 2007 patients were randomly assigned. REMODEL-1 included 1000 patients (remibrutinib 502, teriflunomide 498; mean age 38·2 years, 666 [66·6%] female, 334 [33·4%] male) and REMODEL-2 included 1007 patients (remibrutinib 504, teriflunomide 503; mean age 39·0 years, 675 [67·0%] female, 332 [33·0%] male). ARR was significantly lower with remibrutinib than with teriflunomide: 0·073 versus 0·112 (rate ratio [RR] 0·648 [95% CI 0·453-0·927]; p=0·018) in REMODEL-1 and 0·080 versus 0·116 (RR 0·688 [0·487-0·972]; p=0·034) in REMODEL-2. The most common adverse events were upper respiratory tract infection (132 [13·1%] of 1006 with remibrutinib vs 137 [13·7%] of 1001 with teriflunomide), nasopharyngitis (92 [9·1%] vs 123 [12·3%]), diarrhoea (84 [8·3%] vs 109 [10·9%]), and alopecia (58 [5·8%] vs 135 [13·5%]). Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were less frequent with remibrutinib (31 [3·1%]) versus teriflunomide (58 [5·8%]). The safety profile of remibrutinib was consistent with that in other indications, including no liver safety concerns. Remibrutinib was superior to teriflunomide in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, while maintaining a favourable safety profile. These findings support remibrutinib as a potential new oral treatment option for relapsing multiple sclerosis. Novartis.

articles.title: Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
articles.abstract: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results. A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. articles.title: Immunogenicity and safety of BPZE1, an intranasal live attenuated pertussis vaccine, evaluated with and without tetanus-reduced diphtheria-acellular pertussis vaccine in healthy children aged 6-17 years: a randomised, active-controlled and placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial.
Medical cannabis for the treatment of insomnia.
articles.abstract: Insomnia is highly prevalent and associated with substantial individual and societal burden, while existing pharmacological treatments are limited by adverse effects and concerns about long-term use. The role of medical cannabis in the treatment of insomnia remains unclear because of limited and heterogeneous evidence. Despite increasing clinical use, current guidelines do not provide clear recommendations due to uncertainty regarding its efficacy and safety. A clear synthesis of available evidence is needed to inform patients, clinicians, and policymakers about the potential benefits and harms of medical cannabis for insomnia. To assess the benefits and harms of medical cannabis in adults with insomnia. We used CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Global Index Medicus, and two trial registers, together with reference checking, citation searching, and contacting study authors, to identify studies for inclusion in the review. The latest search date was 5 April 2025. We included parallel randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cross-over RCTs, and cluster RCTs in adult participants with any type of insomnia comparing medical cannabis with placebo, benzodiazepine receptor agonists, benzodiazepines, melatonin receptor agonists, antidepressants, and antipsychotics. We excluded studies that were quasi-RCTs and studies using experimental and unregistered drugs, cannabis receptor antagonists and negative allosteric modulators like rimonabant, as well as modulators that enhance endocannabinoid system activity, such as fatty acid amide hydrolase inhibitors, and synthetic cannabis, like levonantradol. Our critical outcomes were quality of sleep/satisfaction with sleep, total sleep time and adverse events. Our important outcomes included sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, daytime functioning, withdrawal symptoms, and quality of life. We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for parallel RCTs and the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for cross-over RCTs. We synthesized results for each outcome using meta-analysis where possible, using a random-effects model. Where this was not possible due to the nature of the data, we synthesized results narratively. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for our critical outcomes, daytime functioning and quality of life for the comparison of medical cannabis versus placebo. Invasive interval breast cancer rates after digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography versus digital mammography screening (TOSYMA): 24-month follow-up of the multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial.
articles.abstract: Despite high invasive breast cancer detection rates, the effectiveness of digital breast tomosynthesis screening is still uncertain. We aimed to compare the invasive interval cancer rates in women screened with digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised two-dimensional (s2D) mammography with those screened with digital mammography. TOSYMA is a multicentre, open-label, parallel-group, randomised, controlled, superiority trial done at 17 screening sites across two federal states in Germany. Women aged 50-70 years were randomly allocated (1:1) to digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography or digital mammography. The first primary endpoint of TOSYMA (TOSYMA-1) was the detection rate of invasive breast cancer and has been previously reported. The second primary endpoint (TOSYMA-2) was the invasive interval cancer rate, defined as the proportion of women who developed an invasive breast cancer in the 24-month interval after being negative at screening (ie, no ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive breast cancer detection) in TOSYMA-1. The primary endpoint was analysed in all participants with a negative screening result in TOSYMA-1. The cumulative incidence of invasive interval cancers at 12 months in screen-negative women was the prespecified secondary outcome. Suspected interval cancers were identified by data linkage to cancer registries. The study is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03377036) and is closed to accrual but follow-up is ongoing. Between July 5, 2018, and Dec 30, 2020, 99 689 women were enrolled in TOSYMA-1 and 99 558 participants included in the modified full analysis set of TOSYMA-1. The median age was 57 years (IQR 53-62) in the TOSYMA-2 modified full analysis set and all participants were female. 49 299 (99·1%) of 49 762 women assigned digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography screened negative in TOSYMA-1, as were 49 456 (99·3%) of 49 796 women assigned digital mammography who had evaluable data and were included in the TOSYMA-2 modified full analysis set. Invasive interval cancers were detected in 70 of 49 299 women in the digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography group (invasive interval rate 14·2 cases per 10 000 women screened with a negative result) and in 92 of 49 456 women in the digital mammography group (18·6 cases per 10 000 women screened with a negative result; adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0·76 [95% CI 0·55-1·06]; p=0·11). Although the primary outcome of TOSYMA-2 did not reach statistical significance, this large, randomised trial adds substantial evidence to the use of digital breast tomosynthesis plus s2D mammography in breast cancer screening. articles.title: Half-dose rivaroxaban vs antiplatelet therapy for preventing silent cerebral embolism after left atrial appendage occlusion: the HALO-SCE trial.
articles.abstract: The optimal long-term antithrombotic strategy after left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) remains undetermined. The present study aimed to investigate whether half-dose rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) could better reduce silent cerebral embolic lesions (SCEs) and preserve cognitive function compared to antiplatelet therapy after successful LAAO. In this investigator-initiated, prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial, patients with successful LAAO confirmed 45 days post-procedure were assigned 1:1 to half-dose rivaroxaban or antiplatelet therapy group. Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging and cognitive assessments were repeated at 90, 180 and 365 days after LAAO. The primary outcome was the patient-level incidence of any newly detected SCE during follow-up. Secondary outcomes included cognitive trajectories, SCE burden, and a composite of all-cause mortality, clinical thromboembolic events and major bleeding. Between December 2022 and February 2025, 164 patients were randomized. The patient-level incidence of new SCEs was significantly lower in the half-dose rivaroxaban group than in the antiplatelet therapy group (10/82 [12.2%] vs. 26/82 [31.7%]; P = 0.005). At 365 days, model-derived between-group differences favored the half-dose rivaroxaban group for both Mini-Mental State Examination (2.56; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.11-4.01; P < 0.001) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (2.67; 95% CI 1.07-4.26; P = 0.001) scores. The composite clinical outcome occurred in 2.4% of the half-dose rivaroxaban group vs. 11.0% of the antiplatelet therapy group (P = 0.057). In patients eligible for oral anticoagulation after successful LAAO, rivaroxaban 10 mg daily significantly reduced SCEs and better maintained cognitive function compared with antiplatelet therapy, with numerically fewer composite clinical events.

articles.title: Effect of Vasopressin Initiation Threshold on Septic Shock Mortality: The VASSPR Cluster Crossover Randomized Strategy Trial.
articles.abstract: The optimal vasopressor dose at which to initiate a second vasopressor in patients with septic shock is uncertain. To compare the effects of hospital-level strategies initiating vasopressin infusion at a lower threshold vs a higher threshold on outcomes in patients with septic shock. Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026. Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter. The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics. There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]). In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors. articles.title: VERIFY: A Phase III Trial of Rusfertide Versus Placebo in Phlebotomy-Dependent Patients With Polycythemia Vera Receiving Standard-of-Care Therapy.
articles.abstract: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by erythrocytosis. Rusfertide is a subcutaneous, injectable, hepcidin mimetic peptide that suppresses erythrocytosis. The phase III VERIFY trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of rusfertide in phlebotomy-dependent patients with PV and poorly controlled hematocrit. In VERIFY Part 1a (32 weeks), patients requiring frequent phlebotomy were randomly assigned (1:1, double-blind) to receive rusfertide or placebo with or without cytoreductive therapy. The primary efficacy end point was clinical response (absence of phlebotomy eligibility; weeks 20-32). Key secondary end points (baseline to week 32) included mean number of phlebotomies, proportion of patients who maintained hematocrit <45%, and mean change from baseline in patient-reported outcomes (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System [PROMIS] Fatigue Short Form 8a [SF-8a] T score and Myelofibrosis Symptom Assessment Form [MFSAF] Total Symptom Score-7 items [TSS7]). Patients (N = 293) were randomly assigned to rusfertide (n = 147) or placebo (n = 146). Significantly more patients (n = 113, 77%) achieved a clinical response with rusfertide versus placebo (n = 48; 33%;  < .0001). Compared with placebo, rusfertide reduced mean ± standard deviation number of phlebotomies (0.5 ± 1.2  1.8 ± 1.5;  < .0001) and was superior in maintaining hematocrit <45% (n = 92 [63%]  n = 21 [14%];  < .0001). Rusfertide led to a significant improvement in the PROMIS Fatigue SF-8a T-score and MFSAF TSS7 versus placebo ( = .0252 and .0240, respectively). Injection site reactions, anemia, and fatigue were the most common adverse events. No deaths were reported. Rusfertide significantly improved hematocrit control, reduced the need for phlebotomy, and improved patient-reported symptoms versus placebo in phlebotomy-dependent patients with PV who were also receiving standard-of-care therapy.

articles.abstract: Early intensive blood pressure (BP) lowering is now recognized as an effective approach to improve outcome after acute intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). However, whether the effect varies by hematoma location is uncertain. We aimed to determine the heterogeneity of the treatment effect of intensive BP lowering on functional outcome by hematoma location. We conducted a pooled analysis of individual patient-level data (IPD) from all 4 Intensive Blood Pressure Reduction in Acute Cerebral Hemorrhage Trials (INTERACT) and the second Antihypertensive Treatment of Acute Cerebral Hemorrhage (ATACH-II) trial, which were international, randomized, open, blinded end point assessed, controlled trials that investigated the effectiveness of early intensive BP control in acute ICH. ICH location was classified as lobar or deep hemisphere or infratentorial. The primary outcome was death or disability (modified Rankin Scale scores 3-6) at 90 days or 6 months (for INTERACT3). The heterogeneity of the treatment effect of intensive BP lowering on the primary outcome by ICH location was estimated using generalized linear mixed models with trial as a random effect and adjustment for prespecified clinical covariates and an interaction term of "treatment-by-location." Among 11,288 patients (mean age 62.5 years [SD 12.7]; 4,056 [35.9%] women), 1,141 (10.1%) had lobar ICH, 9,202 (81.5%) had deep ICH and 945 (8.4%) had infratentorial ICH. Compared with deep or infratentorial ICH, lobar ICH occurred in older patients, was less often associated with intraventricular hemorrhage, and had larger hematoma volumes (all  < 0.001). The effect of intensive BP lowering on the primary outcome of death or disability differed by ICH location ( for interaction = 0.033). articles.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for Systemic Antibacterial and Antifungal Prophylaxis in Pediatric Patients With Cancer and Hematopoietic Cell Transplant Recipients: 2026 Update.
articles.abstract: To provide updated Pediatric Oncology Group of Ontario clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) for systemic antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis in pediatric patients with cancer and hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) recipients. In this update, we harmonized procedures and recommendations across both the antibacterial and antifungal CPGs. Systematic reviews of randomized clinical trials evaluating systemic antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis in pediatric and adult patients with cancer and HCT recipients were updated. Using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach, an international multidisciplinary panel revised or formulated recommendations and classified evidence quality. Good practice statements were also created. The updated search identified 13 new randomized trials published since 2019 (eight antibacterial and five antifungal), resulting in 195 total trials. The panel maintained a conditional recommendation to consider antibacterial prophylaxis in pediatric patients with AML and relapsed ALL and a strong recommendation to use levofloxacin when antibacterial prophylaxis is planned. A new conditional recommendation was introduced to consider using no antibacterial prophylaxis in patients unable to receive levofloxacin. Strong recommendations to use antifungal prophylaxis in pediatric patients with AML and allogeneic HCT recipients and to use an echinocandin or a mold-active azole when antifungal prophylaxis is planned were maintained. Three new good practice statements were added, focusing on drug interactions, infection prevention practices, and monitoring infection epidemiology. This update consolidates and harmonizes CPGs for systemic antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis in pediatric patients with cancer and HCT patients. Future research should refine prophylaxis indications for different patient subgroups.

articles.abstract: Insulin dose-adjusted hemoglobin A1c (IDAA1c = HbA1c [%] + [4 × total daily dose in units/kg/day]) ≤9 is widely used to define partial remission in pediatric type 1 diabetes and as an eligibility criterion or outcome in disease-modifying therapy trials. However, it has not been validated in U.S. youth. Because higher BMI increases insulin resistance and insulin requirements, we hypothesized that IDAA1c would perform suboptimally in participants with overweight or obesity. Partial remission was defined using MMTT-stimulated area under the curve (AUC) mean C-peptide. Participant characteristics were compared by BMI category (<85th percentile [normal or underweight] and ≥85th percentile [overweight or obese]) using Wilcoxon rank sum and Fisher exact tests. Participants with normal or underweight versus participants with overweight or obesity had lower IDAA1c (8.95 vs. 9.28, P = 0.043) despite lower stimulated C-peptide (1.25 vs. 1.88 ng/mL, P < 0.001). Overall, IDAA1c ≤9 had 61% sensitivity and 79% specificity for predicting C-peptide ≥0.91 ng/mL with an ROC AUC of 0.77. Among participants with overweight or obesity, sensitivity was 45% and specificity 81%. A Youden index-derived cutoff of IDAA1c ≤11.6 improved sensitivity to 93%, with specificity of 54% in participants with overweight or obesity. IDAA1c ≤9 demonstrated suboptimal accuracy as a screening test for partial remission, especially underestimating β-cell function in youth with overweight or obesity. BMI-specific cutoffs improved sensitivity but reduced specificity.

articles.title: Intraoperative Dobutamine Plus Norepinephrine to Prevent Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury in Septic Shock: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: International guidelines recommend dobutamine for management of septic shock and cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion in adults based on very low-certainty evidence. Randomized trials are lacking on the effect of intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine on postoperative outcomes in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control. To determine whether intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) within 7 postoperative days in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control. This randomized, open-label clinical trial in 39 tertiary hospitals in China enrolled adults with septic shock who were undergoing surgical source control between June 2024 and August 2025. Follow-up ended on November 15, 2025. Intraoperative, intravenous infusion of dobutamine (up to 5 µg/kg/min) combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine alone. The primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery, defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The 11 secondary outcomes included Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention. Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. SOFA scores on postoperative day 1 (adjusted difference, -0.53 [95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07]) were lower and urine output 1 hour post intervention (adjusted difference, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07] mL/kg/h) was higher in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group. Stage 2 and 3 AKI were lower in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group compared with the norepinephrine alone group (stage 2: 4.8% vs 9.9%; ARR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.26-0.88]; stage 3: 7.9% vs 13.6%; ARR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.91]). Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone. Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine. articles.title: SGLT2 Inhibitors Reduce Heart Failure Hospitalization, Cardiovascular Death and Kidney Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease are the principal drivers of morbidity and mortality in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have demonstrated cardiorenal benefits in landmark trials, yet cross-trial inconsistencies in cardiovascular mortality, renal endpoints and drug-specific effects leave the class-level estimates incompletely synthesized. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and CENTRAL were searched from inception through 15 May 2026. Large placebo-controlled RCTs (≥ 1000 participants) and prespecified subgroup analyses in adults with T2DM were eligible. The primary outcome was the composite of first hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) or cardiovascular death (CV death). Secondary outcomes were 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), CV DEATH, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, first HHF and composite kidney outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using random-effects inverse-variance models. Fourteen studies (76 969 patients; 41 761 SGLT2i, 35 208 placebo) were included. SGLT2i reduced the primary composite by 23% (HR: 0.77, 95% CI: 0.73-0.81, p < 0.0001; I = 0%), with no effect modification by baseline HF (p-interaction = 0.82) or established ASCVD (p-interaction = 0.46). MACE was reduced by 14% (HR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.81-0.92), driven by significant reductions in CV DEATH (HR: 0.86, 95% CI: 0.79-0.93) and MI (HR: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81-0.96), with no significant effect on stroke (HR: 0.93, 95% CI: 0.81-1.08). First, HHF was reduced by 29% (HR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.66-0.77) and composite kidney outcomes by 31% (HR: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.60-0.79). SGLT2i confer consistent and clinically meaningful cardiorenal protection in T2DM across the full spectrum of cardiovascular and renal risk. The ertugliflozin estimate and the moderate heterogeneity in kidney outcomes should be interpreted in the context of trial-level clinical differences and nonstandardized kidney endpoint definitions. These findings support proactive, guideline-concordant initiation of evidence-based SGLT2i agents by endocrinologists, cardiologists and primary care providers as foundational therapy in T2DM.

articles.title: Petrelintide, a human amylin analogue for the treatment of obesity (ZUPREME 1): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial.
articles.abstract: Petrelintide is a novel, long-acting amylin analogue being developed for long-term treatment of obesity, leveraging a mechanism of action distinct from incretin-based treatments. This phase 2 trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of once-weekly petrelintide versus placebo in people with obesity. This multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involved 32 sites (public hospitals and private clinics) in Poland, Romania, and the USA. Adults aged at least 18 years without type 2 diabetes, with a BMI of at least 30 kg/m or with a BMI of at least 27 kg/m with hypertension or dyslipidaemia, or both, were randomly assigned (5:1) to self-administered subcutaneous injections of once-weekly maintenance doses of petrelintide (1·0-9·0 mg) or placebo for 42 weeks including dose escalation. Randomisation was done via a central interactive response technology system and was stratified by MRI participation. Participants, trial staff, and the study funder were masked to treatment assignment but not to different maintenance doses; masking was maintained by use of identical vials for petrelintide and placebo. The primary endpoint was percentage change in bodyweight from baseline after 28 weeks. Analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose. Missing data were assumed to be missing at random. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06662539) and the Clinical Trials Information System (2024-512549-18) and was completed on Mar 7, 2026. From Dec 9, 2024, to Feb 25, 2025, we screened 714 participants, of whom 493 were randomly assigned and 485 received at least one dose of petrelintide or placebo. 79 participants received at least one dose of treatment with petrelintide 1·0 mg, 81 with petrelintide 2·5 mg, 83 with petrelintide 5·0 mg, 79 with petrelintide 7·0 mg, 82 with petrelintide 9·0 mg, and 81 with placebo. 255 (53%) participants were female, 230 (47%) were male, mean age was 47 (SD 12) years, mean bodyweight 107·1 kg (20·3), mean BMI 36·7 kg/m (5·5), and 419 (86%) were White. Mean percentage change in bodyweight from baseline after 28 weeks (efficacy estimand) was -7·9% (95% CI -9·0 to -6·7) with petrelintide 1·0 mg, -7·9% (-9·0 to -6·7) with petrelintide 2·5 mg, -9·8% (-10·9 to -8·6) with petrelintide 5·0 mg, -9·3% (-10·5 to -8·2) with petrelintide 7·0 mg, and -9·4% (-10·5 to -8·3) with petrelintide 9·0 mg versus -1·7% (-2·8 to -0·5) with placebo. Estimated treatment differences versus placebo were -6·2% (-7·9 to -4·5) with petrelintide 1·0 mg, -6·2% (-7·8 to -4·5) with petrelintide 2·5 mg, -8·1% (-9·7 to -6·5) with petrelintide 5·0 mg, -7·7% (-9·3 to -6·0) with petrelintide 7·0 mg, and -7·7% (-9·4 to -6·1) with petrelintide 9·0 mg. Bodyweight continued to decline to week 42, with reductions of up to -10·7% with petrelintide. The most common adverse event with petrelintide was nausea (79 [20%] of 404 participants vs five [6%] participants with placebo). Vomiting was infrequent with petrelintide (12 [3%] participants vs five [6%] with placebo); active treatment and placebo had similarly low rates for diarrhoea (30 [7%] participants vs six [7%] with placebo) and constipation (28 [7%] vs three [4%] with placebo). No deaths were reported. Petrelintide achieved clinically meaningful weight reduction and had similar gastrointestinal tolerability to that of placebo apart from predominantly mild nausea during dose escalation, supporting further evaluation as a long-term obesity therapy. articles.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Non-Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study. In a 26-week trial conducted at 22 primary care practices in the United States, we randomly assigned adults with type 2 diabetes who were not using insulin to either CGM or routine care (control). The primary outcome was the glycated hemoglobin level at 26 weeks. Key CGM-measured secondary outcomes were tested hierarchically to control the type I error rate. A total of 145 participants were assigned to the CGM group, and 138 to the routine-care group. Participants ranged in age from 21 to 84 years. The mean (±SD) glycated hemoglobin level decreased from 8.8±1.3% at baseline to 7.2±1.1% at 26 weeks in the CGM group and from 8.7±1.2% to 8.0±1.4% in the routine-care group (adjusted mean difference, -0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.1 to -0.6; P<0.001). The mean percentage of time that the CGM-measured glucose level was in the glucose-level range of 70 to 180 mg per deciliter was 21 percentage points higher (95% CI, 16 to 26) with CGM than with routine care (P<0.001). The between-group difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 54 mg per deciliter was -0.17 percentage points (95% CI, -0.27 to -0.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority); the difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 70 mg per deciliter was -0.20 percentage points (95% CI, -0.43 to -0.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.004 for superiority). No severe hypoglycemia events were reported. Among adults with type 2 diabetes that was not being treated with insulin and was being managed in a primary care setting, the use of CGM led to a greater reduction in the glycated hemoglobin level and to a lower risk of hyperglycemia than routine care. articles.abstract: In eastern and southern Africa, approximately 1 million people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and receiving oral therapy do not have viral suppression because of adherence challenges. articles.title: The efficacy of interventions to prevent type 2 diabetes among women with recent gestational diabetes mellitus-First update of a living systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: The increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in the decade following childbirth among women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) warrants early intervention. A prespecified update of a systematic review and meta-analyses published in 2024 was performed, examining the efficacy of interventions to prevent T2DM among women within 5 years of a GDM-affected pregnancy. An updated search on PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science (PROSPERO: CRD4202127989) was conducted on 14 November 2024. The primary outcome was T2DM diagnosis or measures of dysglycaemia with at least 12 months follow-up in women within 5 years of a GDM-complicated pregnancy. A Bayesian approach was adopted with results reported as effect sizes with 95% credible intervals (95% Crl), and posterior probabilities of intervention effectiveness. Nine new publications were identified in this updated search, resulting in a total of 26 publications from 25 studies (n = 7379) included. Of those, four studies involved a pharmacological intervention and 21 evaluated lifestyle interventions. There was a 15% (95% CrI: 0.69-1.04) and 32% (95% CrI: 0.40-1.07) reduction in risk and hazard ratio for T2DM, respectively, with high posterior probabilities (95.0% and 96.0%, respectively). Reductions were observed for other secondary metabolic outcomes (fasting plasma glucose, body mass index, HOMA-IR and total cholesterol). Compared to the original review, this update indicates greater certainty of the efficacy of preventive interventions for T2DM in women delivered during the first 5 years after a GDM-affected pregnancy. Evidence on the efficacy and safety of pharmacotherapy interventions is still limited.

articles.title: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation.
articles.abstract: One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming. To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support. Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets. A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system. Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system. In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.

articles.title: Haemodiafiltration, haemofiltration and haemodialysis for adults with kidney failure.
articles.abstract: Convective extracorporeal dialysis modalities, haemofiltration (HF), haemodiafiltration (HDF), and acetate-free biofiltration (AFB), remove excess body fluid across the dialysis membrane through an interplay of positive and negative pressures and accumulated middle- and larger-sized solutes more efficiently than haemodialysis (HD). This increased removal of larger solutes, combined with the use of ultrapure dialysis fluid in convective dialysis, is hypothesised to reduce the frequency and severity of symptoms during HD and improve long-term clinical outcomes. This is an update of a review first published in 2006 and updated in 2015. To determine the benefits and harms of convective (HF, HDF, or AFB) versus diffusive (HD) dialysis modalities, or expanded HD (HDx), in preventing all-cause and cardiovascular death, cardiovascular morbidity, fatigue, and vascular access problems in adults with kidney failure. We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase and two trial registers up to 3 April 2025. Additionally, handsearching of journals and conference abstract books was performed, and the references of the included studies were reviewed. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing convective therapy (HF, HDF, AFB) with another convective therapy or with diffusive therapy (HD or HDx) for treating adults with kidney failure. Critical and important outcomes included all-cause and cardiovascular death, nonfatal cardiovascular events, fatigue, problems with vascular access, hospitalisation, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 1 tool. We summarised treatment effects using the random-effects model and reported risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous data with 95% confidence intervals (CI). We assessed the confidence of the evidence using the GRADE approach. We identified 62 eligible studies (6897 participants). In total, 54 studies (6525 participants) compared HF, HDF or AFB with HD (both high-flux and low-flux); two studies (24 participants) compared AFB with HDF; three studies (62 participants) compared HDF with HF; and four studies (163 participants) compared HDx with HDF/HD. Convective dialysis, compared with diffusive therapy, likely reduces the risk of death (any cause) (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.96; I² = 0%; 15 studies, 5463 participantss; moderate-certainty evidence due to indirectness) and cardiovascular death (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.92; I² = 0%; 9 studies, 4761 participants; moderate-certainty evidence due to indirectness). Cardiovascular morbidity was likely not different between convective and diffusive dialysis (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.22; I² = 0%; 2 studies, 2074 participants; moderate-certainty evidence due to indirectness). Little to no differences were found between convective and diffusive dialysis on fatigue (MD -0.95, 95% CI -2.50 to 0.60; 1 study, 543 participants; low-certainty evidence due to imprecision), problems with vascular access (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.50; 1 study, 124 participants; low-certainty evidence due to imprecision), hospitalisation (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.37; I² = 0%; 3 studies, 600 participants; low-certainty evidence due to indirectness and imprecision), or physical quality of life (MD 0.66, 95% CI -1.08 to 2.40; 1 study, 538 participants; low-certainty evidence due to imprecision). Direct comparisons between different convective modalities were limited and underpowered to detect meaningful differences. Convective dialysis likely reduces all-cause and cardiovascular death. Effects on nonfatal cardiovascular events, fatigue, vascular access failure, and hospitalisation are inconclusive. Future RCTs should prioritise methodological rigour and could focus on unresolved questions, including the impact of convective therapies on patient-centred outcomes such as symptom burden, HRQoL, functional status, and intradialytic tolerance, as well as investigating barriers to uptake, evaluating health system readiness, assessing cost-effectiveness, and identifying strategies to promote equitable access. articles.title: Benzodiazepine Use Early in Pregnancy and Risk for Congenital Malformations.
articles.abstract: Existing data on malformations associated with benzodiazepine use in pregnancy are conflicting. To assess the risk for major congenital malformations from first-trimester exposure to benzodiazepines. Population-based U.S. cohort study. Medicaid (2000-2018) and Merative MarketScan (2003-2020) databases. Pregnant persons enrolled from 90 days before pregnancy to 30 days after delivery, and their live-born infants enrolled for 90 days after birth. Exposure was defined as at least 1 fill of a benzodiazepine in the first trimester. Primary outcomes were any major congenital malformation and organ-specific malformations previously associated with benzodiazepine exposure. The investigators estimated relative risks (RRs) comparing exposed versus unexposed pregnancies with propensity score fine stratification weights to control for confounders. An RR of 1.3 or higher was prespecified as clinically significant. In total, 51 339 of 2 478 434 (2.1%) publicly insured and 27 779 of 1 750 721 (1.6%) commercially insured pregnancies had benzodiazepine exposure. The adjusted absolute risks for any malformation in exposed versus unexposed pregnancies were 4.0% versus 4.1% for Medicaid and 4.9% versus 4.8% for MarketScan. The pooled adjusted RR was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.96 to 1.03). Associations with organ-specific malformations were not consistently observed in sensitivity analyses, nor was a dose-response relationship observed. Analyses of different benzodiazepines yielded similar results. The risk for selected organ-specific malformations was increased in some analyses of coexposure to benzodiazepines and other psychoactive medications, but a consistent pattern did not emerge. Potential nondifferential exposure and outcome misclassification; analyses restricted to malformations prevalent at birth. No substantial increase in the risk for malformations was consistently identified across data sources. Findings from coexposure analyses were inconsistent and warrant further study. articles.title: Dual direct current external cardioversion in refractory atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Electrical direct-current cardioversion (DCCV) is a cornerstone rhythm-control strategy for atrial fibrillation (AF). Conventional DCCV is less effective in patients with obesity and elevated transthoracic impedance, but the role of dual simultaneous DCCV in refractory AF remains uncertain. We performed a systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis of dual simultaneous external DCCV, with quantitative synthesis restricted to adults with refractory AF after failed single-defibrillator cardioversion. PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception through November 2025. The review followed PRISMA guidelines. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pooled estimates were calculated using a random-effects generalized linear mixed model, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation for sensitivity analyses. Eight studies were included in the qualitative synthesis and seven in the meta-analysis. Pooled cardioversion success was 79% (95% CI, 74%-83%; I = 0%). Ventricular arrhythmias occurred in 1% of patients (95% CI, 0%-4%) and transient bradyarrhythmia in 13% (95% CI, 4%-31%); no deaths were reported. Exploratory subgroup analyses showed no significant differences in success by pad configuration or number of prior failed single-defibrillator attempts. Dual simultaneous external DCCV was associated with high acute conversion success and few reported serious adverse events in refractory AF. However, predominantly observational evidence, single-arm synthesis, heterogeneous procedural approaches, and limited contemporary biphasic data constrain conclusions regarding comparative efficacy, safety, and optimal patient selection. Prospective comparative studies using contemporary biphasic defibrillators are needed to define its clinical role, including evaluation in emergency department and other acute-care settings, before routine implementation.

articles.title: Intensive vs Standard Blood Pressure Lowering in People With and Without Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: There is uncertainty about the effects of intensive blood pressure (BP) lowering on risks of cardiovascular disease and kidney failure in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). To assess the standardized effects of intensive BP lowering on cardiovascular and kidney outcomes overall, and then to assess for effect modification by CKD status. MEDLINE and Embase databases were searched from inception to January 16, 2026. Randomized clinical trials comparing intensive vs standard BP lowering in adults with and without CKD, with at least 1 year of follow-up, were eligible for inclusion. Meta-analyses were performed using inverse variance weighting after standardizing trial results according to the between-group difference in achieved systolic BP (SBP). Differences in relative effects between CKD and non-CKD populations were assessed using χ2 tests for heterogeneity. The primary outcome was major cardiovascular events; secondary outcomes included kidney failure and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)-based surrogate outcomes for kidney failure. We identified 27 studies including 88 830 participants. Intensive BP lowering reduced the risk of cardiovascular events by 15% per 10-mm Hg lower SBP (relative risk [RR], 0.85; 95% CI, 0.81-0.89), without heterogeneity by CKD status. This corresponded to an estimated (SE) absolute reduction of 4.3 (1.2) cardiovascular events per 1000 person-years in individuals with CKD and 2.7 (0.4) events per 1000 person-years in those without CKD. Intensive BP lowering did not affect risk of kidney failure (RR per 10-mm Hg reduction, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.84-1.11) nor risk of 57% or 50% sustained eGFR declines (RR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.83-1.14; and RR, 1.29; 95% CI, 0.94-1.76, respectively), without heterogeneity by CKD subgroup. Intensive BP lowering increased risk of 30% or greater and 40% or greater declines by 42% (RR, 1.42; 95% CI, 1.28-1.58) and 47% (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.30-1.66). Results of this systematic review and meta-analysis indicate that in adults with or without CKD, intensive BP lowering reduced the risk of cardiovascular events by 15% per 10-mm Hg lower SBP and increased the risk of sustained declines in eGFR, without an increase in risk of kidney failure. However, since baseline cardiovascular risk is higher in CKD, the absolute reduction in cardiovascular events was at least as large in this population; therefore, intensive BP lowering should be recommended in people with and without CKD.

articles.title: Pharmacologic Treatments for Female Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis for the American College of Physicians.
articles.abstract: Vasomotor symptoms (VMS) are common in perimenopausal and postmenopausal females. To evaluate benefits, harms, patient values and preferences, and cost-effectiveness of pharmacologic treatments for VMS. MEDLINE ALL, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to 3 March 2026. Randomized trials of at least 8 weeks' duration of eligible medications in females with VMS reporting VMS frequency and severity, menopause-related quality of life (QoL), sleep quality, endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, and/or serious adverse events (SAEs); U.S. Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency labels for additional harms. Data were abstracted by 1 reviewer and verified by a second reviewer. Independent, dual risk-of-bias assessments were performed. Certainty of evidence (COE) was assessed by 1 reviewer and overread by a second reviewer. Ninety trials were included. COE was low to moderate for most comparisons. Compared with placebo, estrogens with or without progestogens, conjugated estrogen with bazedoxifene (CE/BZA), and oxybutynin reduced VMS frequency and severity. Compared with placebo, neurokinin receptor antagonists (NKRAs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), gabapentin, and progestogens reduced VMS frequency but not severity. Estrogen efficacy varied by dose but not route. Estrogens with and without progestogens, CE/BZA, NKRAs, SNRIs, and SSRIs improved menopause-related QoL; gabapentin, NKRAs, oxybutynin, SNRIs, and SSRIs improved sleep quality. Few SAEs were reported. Evidence was insufficient for patient values and preferences. Estrogens with or without progestogens are of high economic value (high COE). The NKRA fezolinetant has low value (moderate COE). Most studies were short-term and were not designed to evaluate SAEs or long-term harms. Observational studies that could address long-term harms were not included. Estrogens reduced VMS frequency and severity and improved QoL (with or without progestogens and with BZA). NKRAs, SNRIs, and SSRIs improved VMS frequency, QoL, and sleep. Estrogens with and without progestogens were of high economic value. Harms data were limited. Little comparative information exists. American College of Physicians. (PROSPERO: CRD42024558116).

articles.title: Revisiting vasodilator strategy in sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema: A meta-analysis of high-dose nitroglycerin efficacy and safety.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of high-dose intravenous nitroglycerin compared with conventional low-dose strategies in patients with SCAPE. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases was performed from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies assessing high-dose NTG (≥100 μg/min or equivalent bolus regimens) in adult patients with SCAPE. Six studies (n = 534 in comparative analysis) were included. No significant differences were observed in intubation rates (RR 0.91; 95% CI, 0.11-7.73), intensive care unit (ICU) admission (RR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.81-1.05), or ICU length of stay (MD -31.29 h; 95% CI, -330.32 to 267.73). Notably, high-dose NTG showed numerically higher estimates of achieving the target systolic blood pressure reduction compared with low-dose NTG (RR 1.70; 95% CI, 0.36-8.10; p = 0.15). High-dose NTG was associated with a modest increase in hypotension risk (RR 1.41; 95% CI, 1.02-1.94). Single-arm analysis demonstrated high rates of symptom resolution (95%) and relatively low intubation (10%) and ICU admission (12%) rates. Subgroup analyses showed rapid improvements in blood pressure, respiratory rate (RR), and oxygenation. High-dose intravenous nitroglycerin provides rapid hemodynamic and symptomatic improvement in SCAPE. However, these benefits do not clearly translate into reductions in intubation or ICU utilization and are accompanied by a modest increase in hypotension risk. Interpretation is constrained by variable low-dose comparator definitions, differing high-dose regimens, and inconsistent reporting of co-interventions.

Use of Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists for Insomnia and the Risk of Falls and Fractures: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Falls are the leading cause of injury in older adults. Sedative-hypnotic use is a known risk factor, but their use for insomnia continues to be common. Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) are a new, potentially safer class of medications for insomnia. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effect of DORAs on falls and fractures. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL from inception to August 2025 for studies reporting falls and fractures in DORA users and non-users. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or observational studies that reported data on falls and/or fractures for participants using DORAs in any clinical setting were included. Citation screening, full-text review, and data abstraction were conducted in duplicate. Random-effects model meta-analyses were conducted. The primary outcomes were the incidence or rates of falls and fractures among adults using DORAs compared to non-users. We also calculated the optimal information size (OIS), which is the minimum number of events needed to detect a clinically meaningful effect. Nineteen studies (10 RCTs, 9 observational, 183,595 participants) met inclusion criteria. Across all studies, DORA use did not increase the risk of falls compared to non-use (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.56-1.04). RCT data suggest a reduction in fall risk (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.35-0.98) not seen in observational studies (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.59-1.31). No association was observed between DORAs and fractures (OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.94-1.18). DORAs do not appear to increase the risk of falls or fractures in adults. Although these findings suggest that DORAs may be safer alternatives to traditional insomnia agents, low event rates, failure to meet the OIS, and limited data in older adults warrant cautious interpretation. Further research is needed to validate these findings and better characterize the relationship between DORAs and falls and fractures, particularly in older adults.
